Twenty Sixth Indian Antarctic Expedition 2006-2008
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 24, pp 129-157
Space Weather Program at Antarctica
R. Tiwari*, P. K. Purohit and A. K. Gwal
Department of Physics, Barkatullah University, Bhopal, India
*School of  Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Newcastle University, UK
ABSTRACT
The use of GPS (Global Positioning System) in diverse areas such as
surveying, enroute navigation and precision approach of aircraft, deformation
monitoring, and various land/marine navigation applications necessitate high
accuracy and availability. In the presence of time varying irregularities in
ionospheric degrades the performance of the GPS receiver. During 26
th ISEA
(Indian Scientific Expedition to Antarctica), the effect of ionospheric irregularities
on GPS performance were studied. This include, standalone GPS receiver
positioning at Maitri, a real time kinematic position on board ship in auroral
storm region. The study shows strong evidence of ionospheric activity affecting
GPS performance in high latitude during auroral storm period.
INTRODUCTION
The Earth’s atmosphere is composed of various gases; these gases
undergo a process of ionization during the interaction of solar energetic
particle with it. This increases electron density in the ionosphere.
However, the ionization phenomenon is prominent in day-time, while the
recombination process occurs in night-time. As a consequence, the
electron density in the ionosphere is not uniform all the time. Having
said, electron density of Earth’s atmosphere does depend on the interaction
of solar energetic particles as a result the electron density differs with the
different geomagnetic latitude. Generally, based on some of the similar
behaviour of ionosphere, the Earth’s ionosphere is divided into three
geomagnetic regions; the low-latitude region (ranges up to ±30º); the
mid-latitude region (ranges between 30º and 55º N or S); and the high-
latitude region (above 60º N or S).
In geomagnetic low latitude region, there exist many responsible
mechanisms for electron density generation such as; (i) equatorial
130
Electrojet; (ii) electrodynamic lifting; (iii) equatorial ionosphere effect
called the Fountain Effect (electron density is minimum at the geomagnetic
equator while from ±10º to ±20º of the equator, and the strongest effect
is around ±10º [Basu et al., 1988]); (iv) high-latitude effect on low
latitude (direct effect of inter-magnetic fields [IMFs]). Nishida ,[1968]
studied a correlation between the IMFs and equatorial electrojet
production. Besides, it varies with solar cycle and day to night; it is
maximum around 1400 LT, furthermore second large peak in the late
evening during the solar maximum period.
The mid-latitude region is least ionospheric disturbed region.
However, there are some significant events and mechanisms responsible
for enhancing ion density in mid latitude region as well, like, the Sub-
Auroral Ion Drift (SAID), which is associated with auroral storms during
enhanced geomagnetic activity. The basic structure of an auroral storm
is oval and it expands equatorward based on the intensity of geomagnetic
storm, thereby transferring ionized energy from high-latitude to mid-
latitude regions. The SAID drift with velocity greater than 1 km/sec is
SAID [Rodger et al.,  1992], with this threshold, the recombination rate
of oxygen [O] more than doubles. Thus, with the frictional heat developed
due to the recombination process, the ion flow is induced upward,
eventually creating a trough in the E layer of the ionosphere. However,
the probability of its occurrences is well correlated with the strength of
geomagnetic storms [Collis and Haggstrum,1988]. The ionospheric trough
at mid-latitude is a night-time phenomenon; it extends for a few degrees
in latitude during the dusk sector.
The geomagnetic high latitude region is above 60º on either side of
the pole, further it is subdivided into three latitudinal ranges; i) auroral
region (59º - 72º N or S); ii) sub-auroral region (49º - 59º N or S); iii)
Polar region (above 72º in N or S). The source of high latitude ionization
is the interaction of solar energetic particle through the Earth’s magnetic
field lines. The Earth’s magnetosphere protects the Earth from high
thrust of solar wind, although the Earth is exposed to the interplanetary
magnetic field (IMF) which lies in the helispheric equatorial plane
(see Figure 1). The orientation of IMF plays very important role in
letting solar energetic particle into the Earth’s atmosphere. Figure 1
illustrates the sketch of solar energetic particle interaction with the
Earth’s atmosphere, in the Figure 1-A, the flow of solar energetic particle
